questions.problem:
Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(3,1)$ where $t=0,$ given that $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖=2,$ and the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ to the curve is

$$
T(t)=⟨-\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}},\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}⟩.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(0)=⟨3,1⟩,$ since the point $P(3,1)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$, ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{3}}},\,\frac{t}{\sqrt{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{3}}}⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{{({0}^{2}+1)}^{3}}},\,\frac{0}{\sqrt{{({0}^{2}+1)}^{3}}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{2}{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=⟨-1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨3,1⟩+2⟨-1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨3,1⟩+⟨-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the equation ${y}^{″}-14{y}^{′}+49y=0$ for $y=y(t),$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda t},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}-14\lambda {e}^{\lambda t}+49{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}-14\lambda +49) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-14\lambda +49 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -7)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and so $\lambda =7$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation.

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{7t}$ and $t{e}^{7t}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $7{e}^{t}+t{e}^{7t}$ is not a solution.

[T]_{B|C}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 7 \\ -4 & 3 & 9\end{aligned}],\,[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Suppose $B$ and $C$ are bases of the vector spaces $V$ and $W,$ respectively. The matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the linear map $T:V\to W$ relative to these bases, and the coordinates of the vector $x\in V$ relative to $B$ are shown above. Find $[T(x)]_{C}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the image of $x$ under $T$ relative to the basis $C$ can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 7 \\ -4 & 3 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is an upper triangular matrix, we have that its eigenvalues are the entries in the main diagonal, that is, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

Also, since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =5.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & -9 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4{x}_{1}+7{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ -9{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 0=0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the augmented matrix $M$ is already in its row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 7 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{2}{9}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{4}(7{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(7(\frac{2}{9}{x}_{3})+2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{32}{9}{x}_{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{9}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{2}{9}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=9,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 2 \\ 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{8}{2}=4.$

Consider the system of linear equations 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5x+8y=-28 \\ 2x+3y=11.\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the unknown $x$ can be written as $x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{|\begin{aligned}5 & 8 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|}$, where ${D}_{x}=$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5x+8y=-28 \\ 2x+3y=11.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant of the coefficient matrix is 

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 8 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to construct ${D}_{x}$, we replace the first column of the coefficient matrix by the right-hand side column of the given system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x} & =|\begin{aligned}\,-28 & 8 \\ \,\,11 & 3\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[9X+4].$

$$
f(x)=\frac{x}{2},\,0<x<2
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[9X+4]=9\text{E}[X]+4
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[9X+4] & =9\text{E}[X]+4 \\  & =9\cdot \frac{4}{3}+4 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$
